name: Kok-Nar
confidence_why: Black 1980, working from his own phonemicisation of Sommer's and Breen's Kok-Nar material, finds stress contrastive (hedged as 'probably') as the continuation of Proto-Norman-Pama vowel length, and Goedemans 1998, summarising Breen 1976, files Kok Narr under initial stress with very frequent stress on the second syllable and no regularities discovered, so the two sources agree on unpredictable placement, but they are only two, one is hedged and the other second-hand, and Breen's sketch itself remains unread.

catalog_locator: p.198 (end of the section on the phonologies of the languages, immediately before the heading '5. Pre-Norman Pama phonology') and p.203 (section 5, vowel length); Kok-Nar data sources p.190; KB/KN e < *a 'in many non-initial syllables that are now stressed' p.202
catalog_quote: [p.198] Stress is contrastive in Koko-Bera and probably also in Kok-Nar and is transcribed acute when attested for a form in either language. Stress is not transcribed for Kukatj, although Breen notes that it could conceivably be contrastive. [p.203] In Koko-Bera and Kok-Nar length would continue as stress: e.g. *nʸa:ka-la > KB, KN ṉákal 'saw (v. pst.)' but *panʸtʸi[:]l- > KB pinʸtʸé- and KN βinʸtʸé- 'be burning'. Kok-Nar in particular however appears to have undergone changes in length or stress - cf. *kuta[:]ka > KB kutéw, but KN kúrək 'dog' ... such forms show no stress contrasts in Koko-Bera and Kok-Nar ... The fact that length appears to be reflected as stress in Koko-Bera and Kok-Nar could suggest that phonetic stress was positively correlated with length in the protolanguage. Alpher (1972:71) has meanwhile maintained that stress fell predictably on the first syllable of 'Proto-Paman' forms.

Black 1980 'Norman Pama historical phonology', PL A-59. p.198 (txt page idx 17) reads exactly: 'Stress is contrastive in Koko-Bera and probably also in Kok-Nar and is transcribed acute when attested for a form in either language. Stress is not transcribed for Kukatj, although Breen notes that it could conceivably be contrastive.' p.203 (page idx 22) reads: 'In Koko-Bera and Kok-Nar length would continue as stress: e.g. *nYa:ka-la > KB, KN nakal 'saw' but *panYtYi[:]l- > KB pinYtYe- and KN [p]inYtYe- 'be burning'. Kok-Nar in particular however appears to have undergone changes in length or stress - cf. *kuta[:]ka > KB kut…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Black, Kok-Nar word stress is (probably) lexically contrastive between the first and second syllable: most words are initial-stressed, but words whose Proto-Paman etymon had a long second-syllable vowel carry stress on the second syllable (e.g. KN nákal 'saw' vs. second-syllable-stressed reflexes of *panYtYi[:]l- 'be burning'); Black marks stress with an acute wherever attested. Goedemans 1998 (App. D p.244, from Breen 1976b) independently files Kok Narr as 'initial stress with very frequent stress on second, no regularities discovered'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Kok-Nar (Goedemans notes initial secondary stress with third-syllable main stress only for neighbouring Koko Bera).
new_statements.exceptions: Black hedges ('probably'); monosyllables show no stress contrast; he warns his Kok-Nar data (last speakers) are heavily contaminated by Kurtjar and Koko-Bera and that some KN forms show unexplained 'changes in length or stress' (e.g. *kuta[:]ka > KN kórak 'dog' with initial stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on cited lexical forms (comparative wordlist data, citation forms); no phrase-level discussion. Statement is an analyst's summary in a historical-comparative paper, not a dedicated synchronic description; the primary sketch (Breen 1976b) was not accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: Black 1980 treats 'Kok-Nar', Breen's 'Gog-Nar', Sommer's kok naŋ and the names kunlar/kuanlar ('Gwandar') as a single language (= Glottolog kokn1236, AIATSIS G29), attributing apparent dialect differences reported by Oates 1975, Sommer 1976 and Breen 1976b to contamination from Kurtjar and Koko-Bera; his Kok-Nar forms come from the last few speakers (only one alive in 1980) and he flags them as less reliable than Breen's. Goedemans 1998 uses the spelling 'Kok Narr' (Tindale T177). Note Black classes Kok-Nar as a non-Norman-Pama neighbour (with Kukatj and Koko-Bera), whereas Glottolog 5.1 files kokn1236 under Norman Pama.

readall_conflicts: No new source could be opened, so no new disagreement. The existing evidence is mildly heterogeneous but compatible: Black 1980 (p.198, p.203) says stress is contrastive in Koko-Bera and 'probably also in Kok-Nar', continuing Proto-Norman-Pama vowel length; Goedemans 1998 (App. D p.244, second-hand from Breen 1976b) files Kok Narr as 'initial stress with very frequent stress on second, no regularities discovered'. Both describe stress whose position is not predictable from syllable count, so 'lexical (unpredictable)' (initial-tending, first or second syllable) stands. The unattributed length-driven stress rule visible in the archive.org volume-level highlights of Sutton (ed.) 1976 must not be read as a Kok-Nar rule: Black 1980 p.203 states that Kok-Nar has no vowel length (length became stress), so a 'lengthened vowel' rule most likely describes another language in the volume.
